prudent.definition: careful and sensible about the future
sentences: The prudent course looked timid for two years and brilliant in the third.
It is prudent to read the clause about renewal before signing anything for a decade.
The editor pruned forty pages and the book breathed for the first time.
Prune the roses hard in February and they forgive you by June.

prurient.definition: having an unhealthy interest in sexual matters
sentences: The coverage was prurient rather than investigative and nobody pretended otherwise.
Prurient interest is the phrase courts use when they mean the audience, not the art.
The fabric puckered along the seam and the whole jacket had to be recut.
Her mouth puckered at the taste before her manners caught up.
The puerile joke in the annual report survived four rounds of review.
Puerile behavior at fifty is judged more harshly and practiced just as often.
Pugilism was illegal, popular, and reported in detail by the same newspapers that condemned it.
The debate descended into intellectual pugilism with nothing at stake.
The retired pugilist ran a bakery and had the gentlest handshake in the town.
He argued like a pugilist: forward, constantly, until somebody stopped.
The pugnacious columnist picked fights with people who had not noticed him.
A pugnacious opening statement lost the jury in the first minute.
The puissance of the old families rested on land and marriage, in that order.
The word survives mainly in poetry and in a showjumping event.
A puissant argument, delivered badly, still lost the vote.
The puissant lords of the charter could not read the document they sealed.
Pulchritude is a strikingly ugly word for a beautiful thing.
The poem praises her pulchritude for forty lines and her wit for none.
The coastline was pummeled by three storms in a fortnight.
Critics pummeled the film and audiences ignored them entirely.
He was punctilious about form and entirely relaxed about substance.
A punctilious host notices what the guests do not and could not name.
The pundits predicted a landslide and the electorate produced a hung parliament.
Pundit comes from a Sanskrit word for a learned man, which the panel shows have diluted.

pungent.definition: sharply strong in smell, taste, or wit
sentences: A pungent aside from the back of the room ended the discussion.
The cheese was pungent enough to be discussed by neighbors.

purport.definition: to claim to be, often falsely
sentences: The letter purports to be from 1854 and uses a word coined in 1902.
The scheme purported to help small suppliers and paid them last.
She pursed her lips at the suggestion, which was the entire review.
He pursed his mouth, said nothing, and the meeting understood perfectly.
Pursuant to the regulations, the form was rejected for using blue ink.
"Pursuant to" is legal English for "because a rule says so."

purvey.definition: to supply goods or spread information
sentences: The shop purveyed cheese, gossip, and the parish's only reliable weather forecast.
The site purveys rumor with the confidence of a wire service.
The pusillanimous statement managed to deplore the event without naming anyone involved.
Pusillanimous means small-souled, which is a devastating literal translation.

putrefy.definition: to rot and produce a foul smell
sentences: The catch putrefied in the hold when the refrigeration failed off the coast.
Unaddressed grievances putrefy rather than fade.

pyrrhic.definition: won at too great a cost
sentences: A pyrrhic victory in the courts bankrupted the firm that won it.
Pyrrhus beat the Romans twice and said one more such victory would finish him.
They quaffed the good wine before the guests who understood it arrived.
Quaff is a word used exclusively in poems and pub names.
The intervention became a quagmire that four governments inherited in turn.
A legal quagmire is one where every exit requires the other party's agreement.
He did not quail at the shouting and folded instantly at the silence.
The junior clerk quailed and then asked the question anyway.
The endorsement came with a qualification that removed most of its value.
His only qualification for the role was having survived the last one.
The report gave qualified support, which the press reported as endorsement.
A qualified yes from that committee is the most anyone has ever received.

qualify.definition: to limit or modify a statement
sentences: He qualified the claim so heavily that nothing measurable remained.
Every sentence in the abstract was qualified twice, which is scientific writing.

qualm.definition: a feeling of doubt or unease
sentences: He had no qualms about the decision and several about how it was announced.
A qualm ignored at the start becomes a chapter in the inquiry.

quandary.definition: a state of uncertainty over a difficult choice
sentences: The quandary was that both options required an apology to somebody.
A quandary with only bad exits is best resolved quickly.
Quarantine takes its name from the forty days Venice made ships wait.
The files were placed in quarantine until somebody could verify their provenance.
The appeal court quashed the conviction after eleven years.
Management quashed the rumor by confirming it in a badly worded email.

quell.definition: to put an end to; to calm
sentences: One clear statement quelled a panic that four denials had fed.
Troops quelled the disturbance and created a grievance that lasted a generation.
The querulous tone of the letters made their legitimate point easy to dismiss.
He grew querulous about the heating and cheerful about everything else.

query.definition: to question or express doubt about
sentences: A junior auditor queried one figure and unravelled the whole quarter.
Nobody queried the assumption for eleven years because it was in the template.

queue.definition: a line of people or items waiting
sentences: The queue for the exhibit was longer than the exhibit.
Britain's genius, it is said, is for forming a queue of one person.
They quibbled over a comma while the deadline passed unmentioned.
One may quibble with the method and still accept the result.
The dispute lay quiescent for six years and resumed at exactly the same sentence.
A quiescent volcano is not a safe one; it is a patient one.
The pub is the quintessential village institution and closes at nine.
Quintessence was the fifth element the ancients believed the heavens were made of.
The quip made the room laugh and the transcript unusable.
A quip is an argument that has been compressed until it sparkles.
The quirky shopfront was photographed constantly and entered rarely.
Quirky is what we call eccentric when we like the person.

quisling.definition: a traitor who collaborates with an occupier
sentences: Vidkun Quisling's name became a common noun within months of his treason.
Being called a quisling is the most permanent insult in Norwegian politics.
The quixotic campaign to save the theater failed and produced two novels.
Don Quixote charged windmills, and the word has meant hopeless idealism ever since.
The diary's power comes from the quotidian detail: bread, weather, a broken shoe.
Quotidian tasks consume the day and leave no evidence of having been done.
The raconteur told the same four stories for thirty years and improved them each time.
A good raconteur knows exactly which detail to leave out.
A radical simplification of the form cut processing time by two thirds.
Radical means "of the root," which is a more precise word than its politics suggests.
His raffish charm opened doors that his references would have closed.
The raffish quarter of the city has been about to be gentrified since 1970.
A raft of new regulations arrived in April and none in the eleven months after.
The announcement came with a raft of promises and one actual date.
He railed against the new system and used it more than anyone.
Railing at the weather is the only complaint with no possible remedy.
The raillery at the table stopped the moment the guest of honor arrived.
Raillery among friends would be assault among strangers.
The portrait spends more attention on the raiment than on the face.
Raiment survives in translations of scripture and nowhere else.
He wore his hat at a rakish angle that his mother described as an affliction.
The rakish schooner in the harbor turned out to be a very expensive hobby.
The ramifications of the ruling were felt in four unrelated industries.
Nobody traced the ramifications because tracing them was somebody else's job.
A simple question ramified into a two-year inquiry.
The pipes ramify under the whole city and appear on no complete map.
Rumor was rampant and the official statement arrived four days late.
Rampant in heraldry means rearing up, which is a livelier image than the usual use.
The ramparts survive; the town they protected does not.
Procedure became the rampart behind which nobody had to decide anything.
The split was managed without rancor, which surprised everyone including the lawyers.
Rancor outlives the dispute that produced it by decades.
A rancorous exchange in the minutes was toned down before publication.
The rancorous divorce cost more in fees than the house was worth.

range.definition: to vary within limits; to roam
sentences: Estimates ranged from eleven to four hundred, which told everyone nothing.
The herd ranges over twenty miles and returns to the same water.
A wide-ranging discussion covered everything except the item on the agenda.
Free-ranging chickens produce better eggs and worse gardens.
The omission rankled for years and was never mentioned once.
What rankles is rarely the decision itself but the manner of it.
He rose from the ranks and never quite forgave those who had not.
The ranks were closing before anyone had established what happened.
Rapacious lending practices were legal, profitable, and eventually catastrophic.
Rapacious comes from seizing, which is exactly the manner intended.
The rapprochement began with a shared taxi and ended a nine-year silence.
Rapprochement between the departments was announced before either had agreed to it.
The children were rapt for fifty minutes, which the teacher noted as a miracle.
Rapt attention is the highest compliment an audience can pay.

rarefied.definition: exclusive and remote from ordinary life
sentences: The rarefied world of the auction room prices things nobody needs.
At that altitude the air is literally rarefied, which is why the metaphor works.

rarefy.definition: to make less dense or more refined
sentences: Altitude rarefies the air and doubles the effort of every step.
The theory has been rarefied until only its authors can apply it.
A rash promise on Monday became an impossible deadline by Friday.
It would be rash to conclude anything from a sample of four.
The treaty was signed in 1997 and ratified, by the last party, in 2011.
The board ratified a decision that had already been implemented.
The rational choice and the popular one diverged, as they often do.
People are rational within assumptions they have never examined.

rationalism.definition: the view that reason is the source of knowledge
sentences: Continental rationalism started from what could be reasoned; British empiricism from what could be seen.
Rationalism built beautiful systems and required experiment to correct them.
He rationalized the purchase within four minutes and regretted it for a year.
We reason our way into decisions rarely and rationalize our way out constantly.
Raucous laughter from the next room made the interview impossible.
The raucous crows in that square are louder than the traffic beneath them.
Fire ravaged the archive and spared, by chance, the catalogue.
Two seasons of drought ravaged an industry that had planned for one.

rave.definition: to talk wildly or with extravagant praise
sentences: Critics raved about a film that audiences left in silence.
He raved for ten minutes about a restaurant and forgot to say where it was.

ravel.definition: to untangle, or to become tangled
sentences: The sleeve raveled at the cuff after one wash.
Ravel and unravel mean the same thing, which is English at its least helpful.
They arrived ravenous and ate a meal intended for twice their number.
A ravenous appetite for detail makes an excellent researcher and a difficult dinner guest.

raze.definition: to destroy completely to the ground
sentences: The terrace was razed in 1968 to build a car park that is now being razed.
Raze means to level; raise means the opposite, and they sound identical.

reactant.definition: a substance that takes part in a reaction
sentences: The reaction stops when the limiting reactant is used up, whatever else remains.
Identify the reactants before blaming the temperature.

reactionary.definition: opposing progress and favoring the past
sentences: The reactionary faction blocked the reform and could not name what it wanted instead.
Reactionary is a description of direction, not of temperament.

readjustment.definition: a further adjustment to changed circumstances
sentences: The readjustment after returning from six months abroad took longer than the trip.
A readjustment of the figures was announced quietly on the last Friday of the quarter.
They reaped the benefit of a decision made by people who never saw it work.
You reap what you sow, though usually in a different field.
The chair rebuked him publicly and apologized in the corridor afterward.
A rebuke from someone you respect lasts longer than any formal warning.

rebus.definition: a puzzle using pictures for words
sentences: The child's rebus of an eye, a heart, and a ewe was decoded instantly.
Medieval seals often used a rebus so the illiterate could identify the owner.

rebut.definition: to disprove with argument or evidence
sentences: The rebuttal was two pages and ended the debate for a decade.
He did not rebut the claim; he simply asserted the opposite louder.
The recalcitrant printer required a specific ritual known only to one person.
Recalcitrant literally means kicking back, like a horse refusing the bit.

recant.definition: to publicly withdraw a former belief
sentences: He recanted under pressure and restated the same view four years later, abroad.
To recant is to unsing: the word contains "cant," meaning to sing.
Let me recapitulate, he said, and spoke for another twenty minutes.
The final chapter recapitulates the argument for readers who skipped the middle.

recapitulation.definition: a summary of what has been said
sentences: The recapitulation at the end of the movement brings the theme back transformed.
A brief recapitulation saved the last-minute arrivals from total confusion.
The recluse published one novel and answered no letters for forty years.
Being a recluse now requires actively deleting things, which is more work than it used to be.

reconcile.definition: to restore friendship or make consistent
sentences: The two accounts could not be reconciled without assuming somebody had lied.
They reconciled after eleven years over a shared dislike of a third relative.
Reconciliation required the truth first, which is why it took two decades.
Bank reconciliation is a much duller word for the same idea: making two accounts agree.
His recondite specialism became suddenly urgent in the spring of that year.
Recondite means hidden away, and the knowledge usually deserves better.
An hour of reconnaissance saved a week of the wrong kind of work.
Reconnaissance before a negotiation means knowing who actually decides.

recourse.definition: a source of help in difficulty
sentences: With no recourse to the courts, they wrote to every newspaper in the county.
Their only recourse was the ombudsman, who had a two-year backlog.

recovering.definition: returning to health or normal state
sentences: The recovering economy grew for three quarters and forgot the fourth.
A recovering patient is often more work than a very ill one.
The defeat was followed by recriminations that lasted longer than the campaign.
Recrimination is what a team does instead of a postmortem.

recrudesce.definition: to break out again after a period of calm
sentences: The dispute recrudesced the moment the mediator's contract ended.
The infection recrudesced in the third week, which the textbooks had warned about.
Recrudescent nationalism surprised commentators who had declared it finished.
A recrudescent rumor is harder to kill the second time.
The error was rectified in the second edition and repeated in the paperback.
He promised to rectify the imbalance and appointed a committee to define it.
The prose is redolent of a decade the author never lived through.
The kitchen was redolent of cinnamon and burnt sugar for two days.
The redoubtable head of department outlasted five reorganizations.
A redoubtable opponent makes you better; a merely difficult one makes you tired.

redound.definition: to contribute to someone's credit or discredit
sentences: The rescue redounded to the credit of a crew that had never trained for it.
The scandal redounded on the people who had tried to conceal it.
They sought redress for eleven years and received an apology and a plaque.
Legal redress is available to anyone who can afford eighteen months of it.
The refectory seated two hundred monks and now seats a conference on mindfulness.
The refectory table was fourteen feet long and had to be built in the room.
The method was refined over nine years into something a student could run.
Refining the question is usually more productive than refining the answer.

reflect.definition: to think deeply; to show or indicate
sentences: The delay reflects a shortage of staff rather than a shortage of will.
He reflected for a week and did exactly what he had intended on the first day.

refractory.definition: stubbornly resistant to treatment or control
sentences: The refractory infection resisted three antibiotics and yielded to the fourth.
A refractory brick withstands heat that would destroy anything ordinary.
The refulgent dome is visible from four miles and photographs badly from all of them.
Refulgent prose is exhausting past about a paragraph.
A single replication refuted a finding that had shaped a decade of policy.
To deny is not to refute, however loudly the denial is delivered.

register.definition: to record officially; to show or perceive
sentences: The complaint was registered and, as far as anyone could tell, filed permanently.
The remark did not register until he was halfway home.

regress.definition: to return to an earlier, worse state
sentences: Under stress the whole team regressed to habits it had spent a year unlearning.
The patient regressed for a fortnight and then improved steadily.
He reiterated the deadline four times and it was still missed.
Reiterating a point in the same words rarely helps; new words sometimes do.
Her rejoinder was quoted more often than the insult that prompted it.
The best rejoinder arrives, as always, on the stairs afterward.

relegate.definition: to demote to a lower position
sentences: The finding was relegated to a footnote and rediscovered a decade later.
The club was relegated on goal difference and promoted, improbably, the next season.
The landlord relented after the third letter and the first from a solicitor.
The rain did not relent for nine days.
Relentless pressure from one journalist forced a disclosure four committees had not.
The relentless cheerfulness of the induction video was itself a kind of ordeal.

relevant.definition: connected to the matter at hand
sentences: Only two of the forty documents were relevant and both were in the wrong folder.
Staying relevant is the polite word for changing before you have to.

relinquish.definition: to give up or let go
sentences: He relinquished the chair and kept every one of its committees.
She relinquished the claim in exchange for an apology in writing.
He relished the argument far more than the subject deserved.
She did not relish the prospect and did it beautifully anyway.
Remedial work on the roof cost twice the original quotation.
The remedial class was renamed four times and worked all along.
It would be remiss not to mention the four people who did the actual work.
The inspector had been remiss and the paperwork, unfortunately, proved it.

remission.definition: a temporary lessening of illness or punishment
sentences: The disease went into remission for eleven years and returned in a fortnight.
Remission is not cure, which oncologists say and patients hear differently.
He remonstrated with the referee for four minutes and was booked in the fifth.
She remonstrated in writing, which turned out to be the only version that survived.
The possibility was remote and the consequence was catastrophic, which is the dangerous combination.
The remote station was staffed by two people and one very determined cat.
The remuneration committee awarded itself a raise in a paragraph nobody read.
Remuneration is the word used when "pay" would sound too clear.

renaissance.definition: a revival of interest or activity
sentences: The town enjoyed a renaissance after the railway line reopened.
Vinyl's renaissance surprised everyone who had thrown theirs away.
The dispute rent the congregation in two and neither half kept the building.
Rending garments was the ancient public sign of grief.

render.definition: to cause to become; to provide
sentences: The flood rendered the ground floor unusable for eleven months.
He rendered the passage into English so well that scholars quote his version.
The renegade officer published the manual and was court-martialed in absentia.
Every renegade insists that the side changed first.
The buyer reneged two days before completion and forfeited the deposit.
Reneging once costs you the deal; reneging twice costs you the market.
He renounced the title, the income, and, less successfully, the habits.
She renounced the theory in print, which almost nobody does.
A modest repast of bread and cheese was described in the diary as a feast.
Repast is a word used mainly by menus that are about to overcharge you.
The act was repealed after nine years and its effects lasted thirty.
Repealing a law is easier than removing what it built.
The repercussions of the decision reached four departments that had not been consulted.
There were no repercussions, which was itself the most alarming outcome.

repertoire.definition: the range of things one can do or perform
sentences: Her repertoire ran to four hundred pieces and one she refused to play.
His managerial repertoire consisted of enthusiasm and, when that failed, more enthusiasm.
She did not repine at the loss and rebuilt from the same foundation.
Repining changes nothing and is, occasionally, all that is available.
The reserves were replenished in the good year and exhausted in the next two.
A weekend replenished nothing, which told him more than the doctor had.
The report is replete with charts and empty of conclusions.
Replete after dinner, nobody had the energy for the actual discussion.
The face in repose gives nothing away, which is why the portrait works.
He took his repose in a chair by the window and defended it fiercely.
The conduct was reprehensible and, the lawyers noted, entirely legal.
Reprehensible behavior in a small organization takes years to name aloud.
Staff feared reprisals and the survey therefore said nothing useful.
The reprisal was disproportionate and produced the next round on schedule.

reprise.definition: a repetition of an earlier part
sentences: The reprise in the final act earns the tears the first version did not.
This year's crisis is a reprise of 2011 with better graphics.
She reproached him gently, which was worse than shouting would have been.
He reproached himself for a decision that four other people had made.
The old reprobate outlived everyone who had disapproved of him.
Reprobate began as a theological term for the damned and became almost affectionate.
Public reprobation followed the verdict and the sentence was unchanged.
His reprobation of the practice did not extend to refusing its profits.
The party repudiated the pamphlet and the pamphlet's author within a week.
The country repudiated its debts and paid for it in credit terms for a generation.
The proposal was repugnant to everyone and adopted for want of an alternative.
Repugnant literally means fighting against, which is what the stomach does.
The kindness was requited twenty years later, when it was needed more.
Unrequited affection is the entire subject of about half of English poetry.
The offer was rescinded an hour before it was due to be accepted.
The rule was rescinded quietly and reintroduced under a different name.
She approved it with reservations that the minutes reduced to "approved."
His only reservation was the entire second half of the plan.
He accepted the verdict with a resignation that alarmed his friends.
The resignation in her voice was the only honest thing in the meeting.
The resilient old system survived a flood, a fire, and four consultants.
Resilient is what we call people after they have had no choice.
She was resolute in the meeting and privately terrified for a fortnight.
Resolute in the wrong direction is worse than hesitant in the right one.
The resolution passed unanimously and changed nothing at all.
New Year's resolutions survive, on average, into the second week of January.
Their resolve outlasted the funding by three years.
One bad week tested his resolve and the second one broke it.

resonant.definition: deep and echoing; evoking strong feeling
sentences: A resonant phrase in the closing paragraph is what people quoted afterward.
The hall is so resonant that speech blurs and singing soars.

resource.definition: a supply that can be drawn on
sentences: Time was the scarce resource and the budget consumed all discussion of it.
The library is the department's most valuable resource and its least defended.
The two proposals cost four and eleven million respectively.
Respectively is the word that makes a sentence require rereading.
A brief respite in the rain let them move everything in eleven minutes.
There was no respite from the noise until the works finished in October.

restitution.definition: the return of something or compensation
sentences: Restitution of the paintings took forty years and outlived every original claimant.
The court ordered restitution in an amount that covered the loss and not the years.
The crowd grew restive in the fourth hour of speeches.
Restive shares a root with rest, which is exactly backwards and entirely standard.
The restrained design has aged better than the exuberant one next door.
His restrained reply was more damaging than any outburst.
A resurgent local industry employed four hundred people within three years.
Resurgent interest in the technique came from an entirely different field.

resurrect.definition: to bring back into use or existence
sentences: Somebody resurrected a proposal that had been rejected twice in the nineties.
The festival was resurrected by three volunteers and a very good spreadsheet.

retainer.definition: a fee paid to secure services
sentences: The retainer bought availability rather than any actual work.
A monthly retainer is comfort for the client and an obligation for the lawyer.
The tariff was retaliated against within a fortnight and escalated for a year.
Retaliating immediately guarantees the next round; waiting sometimes prevents it.

retard.definition: to delay or slow the progress of
sentences: Cold weather retarded the growth by three weeks and improved the flavor.
Excessive caution retarded a project that urgency would have ruined.
A retentive memory for grudges is the least useful kind.
His retentive mind held every timetable in the county and no birthdays.
He was reticent about his own work and generous about everyone else's.
The witness became reticent the moment names were mentioned.
The minister arrived with a retinue of nine for a meeting with three.
A retinue is a measure of status and a permanent logistical problem.
The retiring author gave one interview in forty years and regretted it.
A retiring manner conceals ambition rather well, which is occasionally deliberate.
The retort was so good that both sides quoted it for years.
A retort is also a laboratory vessel, which chemistry students find endlessly amusing.
The paper was retracted after four years and cited for six more.
He retracted the accusation and the retraction ran on page nineteen.
The firm retrenched in October and rehired most of them by March.
Retrenching during a downturn is prudent and, done twice, terminal.
A retrospective of her work filled three rooms and reversed her critical reputation.
Retrospective legislation is generally considered unfair and is occasionally passed anyway.
The website was revamped four times and never once made faster.
They revamped the syllabus and kept every one of its problems.
The revelry lasted until four and the apologies until Wednesday.
Revelry in the street below made the hotel's charm considerably less charming.
He was revered by students and merely tolerated by colleagues.
Revered institutions are the hardest to reform and the most in need of it.
A reverent hush fell over the room, which lasted about nine seconds.
The biography is reverent to a fault and therefore not very useful.
He was lost in reverie when the question arrived and answered it perfectly.
A long train journey is the last reliable place for reverie.
Public revulsion at the images changed a policy that argument had not.
His revulsion was visible and, in that room, professionally unwise.
He rhapsodized about the coastline for an hour and never mentioned the rain.
Nobody rhapsodizes about a thing they use every day.
The review was less criticism than rhapsody, and readers discounted it accordingly.
A musical rhapsody is deliberately free in form, which is the point.
Strip away the rhetoric and one modest proposal remains.
Rhetoric was a discipline for two thousand years before it became an insult.
The ribald verses in the margin were written by a monk with time on his hands.
The speech was ribald, affectionate, and entirely unsuitable for the recording.
The guilt-ridden letter arrived nine years after the incident it described.
A debt-ridden company can still be profitable, briefly.
A rider attached to the bill funded a bridge in an unrelated district.
The contract's rider was longer than the contract.
Speculation was rife and confirmation was nowhere.
The building was rife with damp and charm, in roughly equal measure.
The rift between the founders was denied for two years and then published.
A rift valley forms where the ground itself has given up holding together.
The rigor of the method is what makes the modest conclusion trustworthy.
The rigors of the winter emptied the camp by February.
Nothing riled him like being told to calm down.
The proposal riled a constituency nobody had thought to consult.
The closure sent a ripple through four suppliers and one whole village.
A ripple of laughter crossed the room and died at the front row.

robust.definition: strong and able to withstand stress
sentences: The finding is robust to every reasonable change in the assumptions.
A robust debate is one where nobody has cried yet.
The rococo ceiling has more gilding than the entire rest of the building.
His rococo prose adds four flourishes to every plain statement.
The announcement roiled markets that had been placid for a month.
The river roiled below the weir in a way that discouraged swimming.
The roseate forecast assumed four things, three of which failed.
A roseate account of the sixties omits most of what happened.
The election was a rout that every poll had described as a close contest.
What began as an orderly retreat became a rout within an hour.
A row about parking dominated the parish council for two years.
The row was audible through the wall and, for a while, entertaining.

rubric.definition: a set of rules or a category heading
sentences: The grading rubric was published after the essays had been submitted.
Everything was filed under the rubric of "transformation," which meant nothing.

rudiment.definition: a basic principle or first element
sentences: He learned the rudiments of the trade in nine months and the craft over thirty years.
The rudiments of a plan existed on one napkin.
A rudimentary shelter kept them alive for three nights.
His rudimentary Italian was enough for the market and nothing else.
He came to rue the email he had sent at eleven at night.
You will rue the day, said the villain, who was, on this occasion, right.

ruminate.definition: to think deeply and at length
sentences: He ruminated on the problem for a fortnight and solved it in a queue.
Cows ruminate by chewing again, which is the metaphor precisely.
The fire drill was a ruse to get everyone out while the safe was moved.
It was a transparent ruse and it worked because nobody expected the effort.

rustic.definition: of the countryside; plain and simple
sentences: The rustic charm of the cottage included an outdoor tap and no insulation.
Rustic furniture costs more than the polished kind, which is a modern joke.

sacrosanct.definition: too important to be interfered with
sentences: Friday afternoons were sacrosanct until the reorganization.
The budget line was sacrosanct because nobody could remember what it funded.
The exam had a sadistic final question that no student finished.
Sadistic is named for a marquis whose books are duller than his reputation.
Her sagacious advice was to wait a week, and the problem dissolved in five days.
A sagacious investor is often just a patient one.
The village sage turned out to be a retired accountant with excellent judgment.
Every field has sages, and the useful ones answer questions rather than pose them.
The salient fact was buried on page eleven of the appendix.
Salient means jumping out, which is what the important detail should do.
The town advertised its salubrious air and omitted the tannery downwind.
A less salubrious part of the city has the better food.

salutary.definition: producing a beneficial effect, often through difficulty
sentences: The failure had a salutary effect on a team that had grown complacent.
A salutary lesson is one you would rather have read about.
The donation salved a conscience that a change of policy would have cured.

sanctimonious.definition: making a show of moral superiority
sentences: The sanctimonious editorial was written by a paper that had run the photographs.
Sanctimonious criticism is the only kind that unites its targets.
The committee sanctioned the trip and then sanctioned the person who took it.
Sanction is its own opposite, which makes headlines about it genuinely ambiguous.
He remained sanguine about the deadline until the week it arrived.
Sanguine comes from blood, one of the four humors, and originally meant ruddy.
Four months of uncertainty sapped the department's appetite for anything ambitious.
Sapping a wall meant digging beneath it, which is where the metaphor starts.
A sardonic note in the margin was the only review the draft ever got.
His sardonic humor made bad news survivable and good news suspicious.
His sartorial standards did not survive working from home.
A sartorial disaster at a wedding lives forever in other people's albums.
